newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus AIDS case woman did not pass on virus-doctor.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus AIDS case woman did not pass on virus-doctor.

text.p: An AIDS specialist testifying at the Cyprus trial of a man accused by his British lover of infecting her with the killer virus on Wednesday dismissed defence claims that the woman had transmitted her disease to a third person.
Early in the trial defence lawyers said Janette Pink, 45, who has accused her Cypriot ex-lover of giving her HIV, had in turn passed the deadly virus on to another man.
"A new patient came to our clinic and claimed he caught the virus in Cyprus, and the most probable source was Janette Pink," Evis Bagdadis, a local AIDS specialist, told the court.
"We asked Janette and she categorically denied it... it was also refuted by the analysis carried out," he said, explaining that the tests revealed two completely different strains of HIV.
Pink, from Basildon in Essex, has accused Greek Cypriot Pavlos Georgiou, 40, of giving her the HIV virus, which leads to AIDS, during a three year affair.
She has also said he told her his wife was dying of leukaemia, when she was in fact dying of AIDS.

In a statement given to police and read out in court last week, Georgiou insisted Pink knew he was HIV positive before they started having intercourse. He also suggested she may have had the disease before he slept with her.
Pink, who tested HIV positive nine months after her relationship with Georgiou started, returned to England last year after developing full-blown AIDS.
Georgiou is charged with transmitting the virus through negligence, which carries a jail sentence of up to two years, a 1,500 Cyprus pound ($2,900) fine, or both. He has denied the charge.
Bagdadis, who treated Georgiou and his wife when she was alive, said both had been cautioned about precautions necessary to stop the spread of HIV.
"We do not tell people they cannot have intercourse but that they should take some simple precautions," he said.

Pink has claimed that, throughout their affair, Georgiou never used a condom, one means of minimising the risk of infection. Georgiou's defence is that Pink always insisted on intercourse without using one.
Bagdadis was allowed to testify after a failed bid by defence lawyers to bar the evidence on grounds it could be a breach of medical ethics.
The judge ruled the issue was a matter of public interest and the doctor would be in contempt if he refused to answer questions.
